channel.title: Weekly Worker — Party & Programme (unofficial)
channel.description: Unofficial RSS feed of articles published by Weekly Worker — Party & Programme.

item.title: Question sacred ‘proof texts’
item.description: There are many who tail what they call the ‘movement’ in the name of some supposed ‘anti-sectarian’ orthodoxy. In reality this means refraining from harsh criticism and abiding by bureaucratic speech controls. Mike Macnair adds to last week’s reports of the Historical Materialism conference
item.dc:creator: Mike Macnair

item.title: Thinking beyond the streets
item.description: Momentum is not being maintained and the left is often pointlessly divided. Yet, though the government is playing a waiting game, discontent has not dissipated. Jean Laurel calls for principled unity
item.dc:creator: Jean Laurel

item.title: Two corpses and a minghun wedding
item.description: No annual conference, no branches, no democracy. Now we are told Left Unity has affiliated. Carla Roberts reminds us that traditionally, in China, a ghost marriage sees reburial in a common grave
item.dc:creator: Carla Roberts

item.title: Setting terms in Congress
item.description: Democrats won more convincingly than expected in the midterms, and the DSA now has its eight-strong Bloc in Congress. There is also talk of a presidential run by Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. How to navigate the coming challenges? DSA member Joseph Perez analyses the results and suggests ways forward
item.dc:creator: Joseph Perez

item.title: Strikes, streets and strategy
item.description: There have been massive protests of school and university students. November 5 took things to a higher level by mobilising the trade unions. What needs to happen next? Jean Laurel argues against the idea that rioting is positive, the way forward, something to celebrate
item.dc:creator: Jean Laurel

item.title: Riot, loot and burn
item.description: France’s huge protest movement began with schoolers and now there is the November 5 general strike. Inevitably the disaffected, the backward, the plain criminal see an opportunity. However, says Jack Conrad, the task of Marxists is to raise consciousness, encourage organisation and inculcate discipline
item.dc:creator: Jack Conrad

item.title: Socialist Organiser to Resisting Socialism
item.description: From 1984 till his death, Alan Thornett was involved in almost every broad left front, coalition, alliance and party attempt. All quickly ended in failure, but lessons were never learnt. Mike Macnair concludes his two-part series
item.dc:creator: Mike Macnair

item.title: From militancy to the swamp
item.description: Alan Thornett, June 15 1937-October 9 2026, was one of those genuine rank-and-file leaders, a cadre steeled in the class struggles of Cowley car assembly plant. Having broken with the CPGB, he threw his lot in with Gerry Healy’s increasingly crazy outfit. After that, one failed merger followed another till he found the ‘lovely waters’ of Mandelism. Mike Macnair begins a two-part article
item.dc:creator: Mike Macnair

item.title: Two out of three
item.description: Should we strive to re-establish Comintern? If not, what sort of international organisation do we need and what can we achieve in the altogether famished here and now? Mike Macnair outlines our broad approach. This is an edited version of his Online Communist Forum talk
item.dc:creator: Mike Macnair

item.title: Cockroaches dent Modi’s veneer
item.description: A single tweet turned into a mass movement that removed India’s education minister and shook the BJP regime to its foundations. But where now? David Lockwood looks beyond streets, strikes and protests
item.dc:creator: David Lockwood

item.title: A chink of light
item.description: Politics are still going to the right - recent state elections show that in no uncertain terms. But then there is Berlin. Die Linke is now the biggest party. Should it compromise and form a red-red-green city administration? No, says Carla Roberts. Better, far better, to be a principled party of opposition
item.dc:creator: Carla Roberts

item.title: Re-establish Comintern
item.description: We have been sent this call for international regroupment. What exact form a world party takes in the future is surely a matter for the future. There are, though, some immediate practical steps that can be taken and we will be outlining our thoughts and proposals in the near future
item.dc:creator: Edith Fischer
Elise van der Doelen

item.title: Politics of the firewall
item.description: Has fascism returned with the AfD? No, but we do have a problem with a left that is desperately trying to help save ‘German democracy’ by going into a cross-class coalition government, says Carla Roberts
item.dc:creator: Carla Roberts

item.title: Tribune of the populists
item.description: In its latest relaunch, Tribune takes a further step from its historic Labourism to engagement with populism in all its ghastly forms and manifestations. Paul Demarty assesses the living dead
item.dc:creator: Paul Demarty

item.title: An honest and open culture
item.description: People Before Profit has enjoyed modest success as a loose alliance. But if we really want revolution and socialism it must, argues Anne McShane, aspire to become a programmatically rooted mass party of the working class
item.dc:creator: Anne McShane

item.title: Beyond the ‘Epstein class’
item.description: We need the truth. We need science. Marxists should abjure conspiracy theories about all-powerful cabals, no matter how popular they are on the internet, argues Paul Demarty
item.dc:creator: Paul Demarty

item.title: Going through the left
item.description: The DSA has grown significantly since 2016 and has recently won a string of congressional nominations. Communists have won increasing influence too. Matthew Campbell-Strupp discussed the perspectives of building a mass Communist Party in America at the opening session of CU 2026
item.dc:creator: Matthew Strupp

item.title: Standing for open debate
item.description: ‘No-platforming’ and speech controls are rooted in the cross-class politics of popular frontism and only serve to strengthen the right, argues Mike Macnair. This is an edited version of his talk at CU 2026
item.dc:creator: Mike Macnair
